rationale: While computational facial phenotyping methodologies played a key role in the discovery and phenotypic delineation of KLHL20-related neurodevelopmental disorder (Sleyp et al., 2022), the primary literature explicitly characterizes the craniofacial dysmorphism as subtle rather than an overt, obligate clinical hallmark. Furthermore, clinical cohorts demonstrate variable multisystemic features (including cardiac anomalies, hypotonia, and cerebellar atrophy) alongside early-onset seizures, and evidence is lacking to establish that facial metrics alone provide an obligate, standalone diagnostic separator from clinically overlapping non-syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.

evidence.text: Facial phenotyping alongside next-generation sequencing was leveraged in medical genetics cohorts to identify and characterize KLHL20 as a novel disease gene associated with intellectual disability and facial dysmorphism.
